notes.text: Port city in the south of France where the story opens. French spelling Marseille; the final s is silent.
Morrel’s three-masted merchant ship, returning from Smyrna, Trieste and Naples.
Island off Italy where Napoleon lives in exile, and its main port.
The ship’s officer in charge of cargo, trade and accounts. Danglars’s job.
Fortress on a small rock in the sea off Marseilles.
Used as a prison for political prisoners.
A small island. Edmond once proposed stopping there with Danglars to settle a quarrel.
Where Faria says the Spada treasure lies hidden, in caves.
A deserted, roughly cone-shaped rock between Corsica and Elba. Edmond has often sailed past it and once landed there.
The Catalan village just outside Marseilles, where Mercédès lives.
Settled long ago by people from Spain, who keep their own language and customs and marry among themselves.
An inn near the Catalans with an arbour, where Danglars and Caderousse sit and drink.
Edmond and Mercédès hold their wedding feast here.
French money. A franc is 20 sous; a louis is a gold coin worth 20 francs.
A crown is three francs, so Edmond’s offer of a hundred crowns to the jailer is 300 francs.
Street in Marseilles where Old Dantès lives.
A supporter of Napoleon. With the Bourbon king back on the throne, being thought one is dangerous; the king’s supporters are royalists.
The crown prosecutor, called “the king’s attorney” in this translation. Danglars addresses his letter to him.
Villefort is his deputy in Marseilles.
Member of a moderate republican faction in the French Revolution. Many were sent to the guillotine in the Terror.
Latin: “let arms yield to the toga”, meaning soldiers give way to civil authority.
The league of European monarchs against Napoleon. The dinner guests have heard it plans to move him from Elba to Saint Helena, far off in the South Atlantic.
Street in Paris. The letter from Elba was addressed to Noirtier at No. 13.
The law courts of Marseilles. Villefort’s house adjoins them, and Edmond is held there.
Secret revolutionary societies in Italy and France.
A member of France’s military police.
French title for a priest.
The royal palace in Paris.
The king’s “closet” is his small private study there.
The minister of justice, who can see the king at any hour.
Royalist nickname for Napoleon, who was born on Corsica. Royalists also call him “the usurper”.
Not electric: a chain of towers with moving arms that relayed signals across France in a few hours.
Bay near Antibes on the south coast of France, where Napoleon lands on 1 March 1815.
France’s highest order of merit, founded by Napoleon. The king gives Villefort his own cross.
Old measure of distance, about 4 km (2.5 miles).
Street in Paris where General Quesnel had an appointment the night he vanished.
A Bonapartist club meets there at No. 53. Noirtier is its vice-president.
Napoleon’s return to power in 1815, ended by his defeat at Waterloo in June.
Fortresses used as state prisons. Villefort names them to Morrel as places Edmond may have been sent.
Faria was held at Fenestrelle for three years before the Château d’If.
Port on the Italian coast opposite Elba, where Faria was arrested.
Fast days, when Catholics ate fish instead of meat. Faria makes pens from the fish.
A fit in which the body goes rigid and seems dead. Faria suffers from it and keeps a red drug to revive him.
A priest’s book of daily prayers. The Spada breviary was handed down in the family, with the cardinal’s will inside it.
Invisible ink that appears when heated. Faria found the will when he used the paper to light a candle.
Old medical term for madness on a single subject. The doctor’s verdict on Faria and his treasure.
Strong, cold north-westerly wind of southern France.
A shroud. Here, the sack Faria’s body is sewn into.
